headers: It is our pleasure to publish the Digital Education Council AI in Higher Education Global Survey 2026, our most comprehensive study of AI in higher education to date, drawing on more than 45,000 responses from students and faculty across 35 countries. The picture it reveals should give leaders pause. AI has moved into the mainstream of student and faculty life faster than institutions have been able to respond to it. Adoption is now widespread, but coherent practice is not. Most students cannot say whether their assessments permit AI or what their programmes are doing to prepare them for an AI-shaped workforce. Most faculty are adapting on instinct, without the frameworks or institutional support to redesign with intent. The result is a vacuum where clear institutional direction should be, and in that vacuum a narrative is forming on its own. Nowhere is this more visible than in the US & Canada, where the data diverges sharply from the rest of the world. As faculty elsewhere lean into AI, confidence in the region is falling and a significant share of students would

headers: faculty views on institutional AI guidance

records.column_1: In 2025, faculty views on institutional AI guidance were already cautious. 40% disagreed that their institution’s AI guidelines were comprehensive, while a further 40% were neutral. In 2026, faculty perceptions remain mixed. Only 37% agree that their institution’s AI guidelines are practical and easy to apply, while 39% remain neutral and 25% disagree. This suggests that the challenge has shifted from whether AI guidelines exist to whether they provide usable direction for teaching practice. Institutions may be developing AI policies, but many faculty have yet to experience them as clear, practical guidance.

headers: This pillar aims to develop learners’ understanding of key technical domains that underpin AI systems, such as data literacy, machine learning (ML), natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision (CV). While the curriculum remains focused on AI literacy, this pillar aims to ensure students can grasp how AI tools function and understand the training and development process of AI tools at a broad level.

records.Pillar 2 Essential AI Concepts: Pillar 3 Social Impact and Ethics of AI
records.This pillar aims to develop learners’ un: This pillar aims to raise learners’ awareness of AI’s profound impact on society and its applications across various sectors while highlighting potential risks and key ethical considerations. This includes understanding concepts of bias, fairness, accountability, privacy, cybersecurity, digital identity and transparency and their role in AI systems. Through this pillar, learners will build values, beliefs and ethical reasoning capabilities to assess when and how to engage with AI tools purposefully, responsibly and safely.

This pillar aims to develop learners’ ability to use AI tools effectively and responsibly in real-life contexts, such as for learning and school project work, communication and creative expression. It emphasises the importance of critical thinking, encouraging learners to evaluate AI-generated content thoughtfully and to avoid over-reliance on AI. Learners will be introduced to methods for verifying information, recognising AI’s limitations and understanding the importance of questioning sources. This pillar ensures that learners are equipped to engage with AI in ways that preserve human accountability and agency, emphasising the importance of keeping human agency at the center of decision-making.

headers: This pillar helps teachers build a foundational awareness of AI by exploring its history, core concepts, types, and the distinguishing factors between AI and human intelligence. It introduces additional topics contextualised specifically for teachers, such as AI’s potential to transform classroom practices and educational administration, while also debunking myths and addressing common misconceptions to build confidence and comfort before delving into essential concepts of AI. Teachers are encouraged to reflect on their evolving role in an AI- enabled classroom, and understand why AI literacy is essential for their professional growth and for guiding students.

records.This pillar helps teachers build a found: This pillar aims to develop teachers’ understanding of key technical domains that underpin AI systems, such as data literacy, machine learning (ML), natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision (CV). While the curriculum remains focused on AI literacy, this pillar aims to ensure teachers can grasp how AI tools function and understand the training and development process of AI tools at a broad level. These topics are aimed at developing a theoretical understanding of AI concepts, while ensuring that teachers can understand and explain how AI tools function and recognise their applications in daily life.

records.Pillar 1 Understanding AI: Pillar 3 Social Impact and Ethics of AI
records.This pillar helps teachers build a found: This pillar raises teachers’ awareness of the wider social, ethical, and environmental impact of AI on society while highlighting potential risks and key ethical considerations. This includes understanding concepts of bias, fairness, accountability, privacy, cybersecurity, digital identity and transparency and their role in AI systems. By examining real-life examples, teachers develop the ability to reflect critically, evaluate risks, and foster ethical reasoning. This equips them to use AI responsibly themselves and to nurture similar values in their students.

This pillar equips teachers with practical strategies to use AI effectively in classrooms, school administration, creative projects, and professional development. It emphasises prompting skills, critical evaluation of AI- generated outputs, and an understanding of AI’s limitations. Teachers learn how to guide students in using AI for learning and problem-solving, while also leveraging AI to streamline their own work and enhance teaching efficiency. The pillar reinforces the teacher’s role as a guide and mentor, ensuring that AI use always keeps human judgment and agency at the center.

headers: Education departments and state curriculum bodies can adopt the AI Literacy curriculum framework as part of their state-level AI literacy or digital literacy initiatives. The framework outlines the curricular structure and progression and enables states to integrate AI literacy into existing subject curricula or introduce it as a standalone module for middle and high

records.Education departments and state curricul: school students and teachers. Education service providers, teacher training institutions and NGOs can use the AI literacy curriculum and content library in their programs to enhance digital literacy, foundational AI awareness or 21st-century skills, especially in government and affordable private schools.

Publishers and EdTech content developers can adopt the AI literacy curriculum framework to design textbooks, digital modules, and learning products aligned to the AI Samarth learning outcomes by customising the topics and sub-topics to cater to different boards, languages and learner needs.

Schools and school networks of both government and private schools may leverage the AI literacy curriculum as a guiding framework for gaining knowledge and awareness on AI Literacy. Teachers can deliver lessons as part of STEM, Information & Communication Technology (ICT) or computer science periods.

headers: Alfabetización mediática para la integración educativa de la IA Propuesta formativa para docentes En un contexto mediático y educativo marcado por la so- breabundancia de contenidos, la automatización de tareas y la expansión acelerada de la inteligencia artificial, esta obra ofrece una propuesta formativa rigurosa, crítica y aplicada para el profesorado. Lejos de concebir la IA como una simple herramienta, el libro la sitúa como un fenómeno cultural, tecnológico y pedagógico que redefine la manera en que se produce, distribuye y comprende el conocimiento. A lo largo de siete módulos, el texto articula un itinerario que combina fundamentos técnicos accesibles con una sólida reflexión ética, mediática y didáctica. Desde la comprensión de algoritmos, datos y modelos de aprendizaje automático, hasta el análisis de sesgos, la gobernanza algorítmica o el im- pacto de los deepfakes, la obra proporciona claves para inter- pretar críticamente los sistemas inteligentes que ya operan en las aulas. El núcleo de la propuesta reside en la alfabetización me- diática como eje integrador: una competencia imprescindible para formar ciudadanos capaces de analizar, evaluar y crear información en entornos mediados por IA. En este sentido, el libro no solo interpela al docente como usuario de tecno- logía, sino como profesional que toma decisiones fundamen- tadas, preserva su juicio pedagógico y promueve prácticas educativas más justas, inclusivas y reflexivas. Con un enfoque eminentemente práctico, cada módulo incorpora actividades, estrategias didácticas y orientaciones de evaluación transferibles al aula. Esta obra se presenta así como una guía imprescindible para quienes buscan integrar la inteligencia artificial en educación sin renunciar a una mi- rada crítica, ética y humanista.

records.Definition: Teacher professional development programs must create a vision for using generative AI. This vision should outline how to train future educators to use AI tools effectively in the classroom and determine which parts of the professional development process itself can be automated with AI to enhance learning.
records.Key questions to ask: 1. What best practices are being implemented by schools to use GenAI to train teachers? 2. What are the risks if schools do not prepare teachers to use AI?

records.Definition: Once a vision for AI has been established, professional development programs must create the execution strategy. This plan should focus on preparing faculty to teach with AI. It must set goals for improving faculty’s AI knowledge and integrating AI in the national curricula. Furthermore, the strategy needs to define the skills that new teachers must develop to prepare their own students for learning in an AI-enhanced environment.
records.Key questions to ask: 1. What are the biggest challenges teachers face when it comes to using AI? 2. What professional learning resources can be made available to faculty to deepen their understanding of AI?

records.Definition: Teacher professional development programs should establish continuous oversight through collaboration to effectively guide AI implementation in schools. Working with partner schools and other organizations is crucial for aligning goals and sharing knowledge. This collaboration creates a supportive ecosystem that ensures ongoing improvement in the use of AI for education.
records.Key questions to ask: 1. What measures will be used to evaluate the success and impact of GenAI initiatives? 2. How can we ensure that the governance group remains inclusive of all relevant perspectives?

records.Key priority: Ensure coherence between national AI strategies and the actual tools deployed in schools, by strengthening governance structures that coordinate MoNE, EdTech firms, and universities.
records.Specific steps moving forward: 1. Create a National AI-in-Education committee to align the National AI Strategy, the AI in Education Action Plan, and MoNE’s digital platforms (EBA, MEBBİS, ÖBA). 2. Develop a unified technical architecture for all AI tools used in schools to ensure interoperability. 3. Institutionalize a sandbox for AI innovation, allowing com- panies to test tools with anonymized datasets under MoNE supervision. 4. Publish annual progress reports tracking implementation, adoption, and impact of AI tools across provinces.

records.Key priority: Reinforce the pedagogical role of teachers in an AIenabled classroom and promote AI literacy among teachers and students so they can use tools responsibly.
records.Specific steps moving forward: 1. Develop national design guidelines for AI tools that ex- plicitly define what tasks AI should and should not per- form in classrooms. 2. Integrate AI-supported pedagogy modules into teach- er training programs, focusing on co-teaching models (teacher + AI assistant). 3. Incorporate AI literacy within the curricula, teaching re- sponsible use, critical evaluation of AI outputs, and aca- demic integrity.

records.Key priority: Strengthen transparency and accountability in all AI-supported assessments, while ensuring compliance with KVKK and ethical AI standards.
records.Specific steps moving forward: 1. Develop a national framework for AI in assessment, in- cluding transparency requirements and audit procedures. 2. Mandate bias testing reports for any AI tool used in grad- ing or student evaluation. 3. Provide KVKK-compliant data governance templates for schools and EdTech companies to ensure lawful process- ing of student data.

records.Key priority: Use AI to address structural inequities, not just classroom-level tasks. Strengthening data infrastructure is key to support predictive analytics.
records.Specific steps moving forward: 1. Define national indicators for dropout risk, combining academic, behavioral, and socio-emotional data. 2. Train school counselors and administrators on interpreting risk scores and designing targeted interventions. 3. Integrate EWS outputs into MoNE’s case-management systems, ensuring follow-up actions are tracked and evaluated. 4. Develop a national research partnership with universities to continuously refine predictive models and monitor unintended consequences.

records.Key priority: Build AI-ready teaching competencies across all provinces and shift pedagogy toward higher-order skills that AI cannot replicate.
records.Specific steps moving forward: 1. Expand ÖBA’s AI training modules into a structured, multi-level certification pathway (beginner → intermediate → advanced). 2. Integrate AI competencies into pre-service teacher education, ensuring new teachers enter the system AI-literate. 3. Develop model lesson plans and classroom scenarios showing how teachers can use AI for differentiation, feedback, and proj- ect-based learning. 4. Ensure rural and disadvantaged schools receive targeted sup- port to avoid widening the digital divide.

records.Box 5.1. Comparing different approaches: Table 5.1 presents some of the advantages and disadvantages of a team-based approach relative to
that of single co-ordinator. The success of a team-based approach appears to hinge heavily on effective
implementation. System and school leaders are important here in ensuring clear, well-defined task
There is though always a degree of ‘unknown’ in team-based approaches as the collaborative nature
depends partly on how individuals can work together, which may not be totally predictable. While efforts
to support development of collaborative and communication skills can be put in place, individual
characteristics will also always have some influence here in shaping the effectiveness of the approach.
Similarly, cutting across approaches is the question of resources and what may, or may not, be feasible
with regard to organising ICT co-ordination in schools.

records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: ACCESS Student E-Readers within Structured Pedagogy in Kenya (Piper et al 2016) E-readers loaded with 100+ digital books (textbooks and storybooks) were provided to Grade 2 learners as part of a structured pedagogy program (Primary Math and Reading, PRIMR). Learners used them daily during school hours as part of regular lessons alongside print books, while teachers continued with regular PRIMR lesson delivery. Teacher and supervisor tablet arms were also tested, providing digital lesson tools and observation guides. The intervention required devices, charging facilities, and training for teachers/supervisors. This model was compared to business-as-usual classrooms without the structured pedagogy program. *Cost: About US$40 for student e-readers (US$0.10 per pupil for supervisor tablets; US$3 for teacher tablets). Samples: 80 schools and 1,580 students in total.
• Content access • Practice
records.TECHNOLOGY CAPABILITIES APPLIED: • Offline storage and access (digital books) • Basic connectivity (initial loading of content, not daily use)
records.EFFECTIVE TPD TRAITS INTEGRATED: • Clear objectives (aligned with PRIMR lessons) • Active, independent student reading
records.OUTCOMES OBSERVED: ▲English reading fluency ▲Kiswahili reading fluency ▲More learners meeting national reading benchmarks

records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: ACCESS SMS-Based Literacy Lessons (M-Shule) in Kenya (Jordan et al 2025) An SMS platform delivering adapted Tusome literacy lessons and quizzes to Grades 1–3. Learners received short texts and quizzes, with answers logged automatically; performance determined progression or remedial review. Parents received reminders. Implemented as a supplemental tool alongside regular schooling after COVID-19 reopening. Required only basic mobile phones (no internet). Compared to control learners attending reopened schools without SMS lessons. *Cost: US$22.70 per standard deviation (SD) gain. Samples: 829 students in total analyzed via server logs, with a subsample of 179 students (94 treatment and 85 control) participating in the experimental trial.
• Content access • Practice • Engagement
records.TECHNOLOGY CAPABILITIES APPLIED: • Connectivity • Interactivity (quiz responses) • Data processing (auto- scoring, adaptive progression) • Transmission and storage
records.EFFECTIVE TPD TRAITS INTEGRATED: • Clear objectives • Active learning • Timely feedback (immediate scoring and adaptive progression)
records.OUTCOMES OBSERVED: ▲Reading (letter recognition, word, paragraph, story reading, and comprehension) ▲Engagement (over half completed at least one subtopic)

records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: ACCESS SMS-Based Reading Support in Zambia (Ome and Menendez, 2022) An SMS-based program delivering short story segments and comprehension questions to Grade 2–3 learners through caregivers’ basic mobile phones. Caregivers read with children three times per week, supported by SMS reminders and monthly facilitator meetings. Voice messages were included but were more costly and less central. The program required only basic phones, caregiver engagement, and minimal facilitation, with no internet or school-based resources. This model was compared to control schools with business-as-usual instruction. *Cost: US$20–22 per child for estimated nationwide scaling; SMS ≈15% of costs. Samples: 80 schools and 2,397 students in total. Longitudinal analysis.
• Content access • Practice • Engagement

records.EFFECTIVE TPD TRAITS INTEGRATED: • Clear objectives • Active learning (child reads and responds with caregiver) • Formative assessment (comprehension checks) • Social-emotional support (reminders and shared reading)
records.OUTCOMES OBSERVED: ▲Oral fluency ▲Listening comprehension ▲Reading (including letter and nonword decoding, word recognition, reading comprehension) ▲Frequency of home reading (alone and with caregiver)

Control groups played a math game to equalize screen time. *Cost not reported. Samples for the 2024 study: 1 school and 60 students. Samples for the 2018 study: 1 school and 31 students. records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: MANAGEMENT Digital textbook tracking platforms (Track-and-Trace) (Bun et al 2024; Read, 2017 These systems replace paper-based textbook ordering with a simple digital workflow usable on basic phones. Schools submit textbook requests through SMS/IVR or a short mobile form; shipments are tagged with barcodes; and school directors or community members confirm receipt digitally. Systems require basic phones, periodic training for school staff, and minimal data connectivity for syncing. *Cost: Not reported.
• Distribution

Learners com-plete tasks individually on tablets or school computers. Teachers and supervisory teams use the stored samples and scores to verify reading levels and monitor progress.
records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: • AI-based oral reading assessment

records.EDTECH TOOL: ASSESSMENTS ABRA (Abrami et al 2016) A literacy software suite with short built-in assessments across phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, and comprehension. The teacher module compiles activity-level performance summaries used by teachers to monitor literacy progress and guide grouping or practice.
records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: • Built-in assessments • Embedded literacy assessments

records.EDTECH TOOL: ASSESSMENTS GraphoLearn (Bora et al 2024) A phonics-based reading environment that captures subskill data every time learners complete activities. Automatically records performance in letter–sound knowledge, rime-unit recognition, and word recognition. Used by teachers and researchers to track reading development.
records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: • Built-in assessments • In-game subskill assessment

records.EDTECH TOOL: ASSESSMENTS onebillion apps (Pitchford et al 2019) Numeracy learning apps that include short quizzes at the end of each topic. The apps verify mastery before learners progress and award completion certificates. Activity data helps teachers or project teams verify foundational numeracy skills.
records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: • Built-in assessments • End-of-topic numeracy quizzes

records.EDTECH TOOL: ASSESSMENTS ProFuturo CAL (Cardim et al 2023) A computer-assisted learning platform with end-of-module checks in literacy and numeracy. Generates item-level feedback and teacher-facing reports used to track individual and class progress and guide follow-up support.
records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: • Built-in assessments • Performance reports and feedback

records.EDTECH TOOL: MONITORING M-Shule (Jordan et al 2025) An adaptive SMS learning system that records learner responses, quiz attempts, and subtopic completion through server logs. Generates engagement patterns and unit-level proficiency scores used by teachers to track participation and mastery in literacy.
records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: • Engagement and usage monitoring • SMS-based en-gagement and proficiency logging

records.EDTECH TOOL: MONITORING Interactive Voice Response (Wang et al 2023) An IVR delivery model for audio lessons in literacy and nu-meracy. The system logs which caregiver–child pairs access each lesson, how often, and how they respond to short comprehension quizzes. Used by program implementers to monitor access and learning dosage.
records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: • Engagement and usage monitoring • IVR-based attendance and quiz logging

Used by teachers and project teams to observe learning patterns and identify skills
records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: • Engagement and usage monitoring • Gameplay log data in numeracy

records.Macro-critical view (Acemoglu, 2024): This view cautions against placing too much emphasis on automation and the replacement of human tasks. The author predicts modest macroeconomic growth (a maximum of 0.71% growth in total factor productivity over ten years) and fears that AI will primarily widen the gap between capital and labour (Acemoglu, 2024). For education, the takeaway is that we must avoid prepa- ring students for roles that AI can perform “adequately” but that devalue human worth – hence Acemoglu’s call for innovation to be directed in a desirable way (Acemoglu, 2024).
records.Micro-optimistic view (Brynjolfsson, 202: By contrast, this approach emphasises the significant productivity gains achieved in the workplace. Experiments showed that average productivity increased by 14% (15% in the 2025 study), with peaks of up to 35% among less experienced employees (Brynjolfsson et al., 2023; 2025). In this view, AI is seen as an “augmentation technology” that helps to boost the performance of employees, particularly those with lower levels of education. Brynjolfsson’s research highlights the potential for inclusive growth in the work- place, as those with lower levels of educa- tion benefit disproportionately more from the use of AI, while Acemoglu’s perspective serves as a reminder of the need to continue investing in human capital.

records.Substitution (displacement effect): AI takes over tasks entire- ly. In earlier automation processes, this involved physical routine tasks (e.g. assembly line work). In the context of AI, this refers to routine cognitive tasks; activities that are frequently repeated, follow a set of fixed steps and require little creativity or deep thinking (e.g. writing meeting min- utes, basic programming work, translation).
records.Complementarity (productivity effect): AI speeds up the perfor- mance of a task or makes it more efficient, which in turn makes people more produc- tive. Humans remain “in the loop”, but perform better (e.g. teaching staff using AI to create personalised les- son plans more quickly).
records.Creation of new jobs (reinstatement effe: AI creates new and more complex tasks that need to be carried out by humans (e.g. verifying or curating AI output, prompt engineer- ing or providing personal guidance, for which there is more time as administrative tasks are eliminated).

headers: There are no specific requirements for top management’s skills in the AI Act, but it would be beneficial if top management, like the rest of the organization, has a basic understanding of what AI is and of the consequences of implementing AI systems in the organization.

Top management should understand the organizational changes and the economic consequences that the introduction of AI systems in the workplace can entail. Top management should be able to allocate the necessary resources for upgrading of AI literacy.

It is positive if the support can contribute to more equal treatment under the law and fewer reasons to complain. headers: FOCUS AREA FOR THE STAKEHOLDER GROUP

records.DESCRIPTION: The organization, department, or person responsible for developing and operating an IT system. For example, a technical or organizational project manager.
A user who has direct interaction with the system. An example could be an insurance advisor handling a case using the system, or a citizen using an online self-help service.

People who do not interact directly with the system but are affected or perceive themselves to be affected by the effects of using the system. An example could be customers whose insurance terms are changed based on other customers’ cases settled by an IT system.

People who may be indirectly affected by the effects of the system or if the system is used in a context of general public interest. An example could be that the general insurance terms across the industry change based on the use of the system.

Companies or individuals who act as suppliers of parts of an IT system or the whole system. This also includes data suppliers. Suppliers can be involved in all phases of a project (see Figure 1). This could be, for example, a supplier of analysis components for estimating insurance risks or a supplier of data for a construction project management system.

records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: ACCESS Offline TPD Module and Remote Coaching in South Africa (Cilliers et al 2022) Teachers received tablets preloaded with scripted lessons and asynchronous TPD modules that included video modeling, interactive quizzes, and content aligned with the national curriculum. Support included biweekly coaching calls, SMS reminders, and peer-to-peer sharing via WhatsApp. This model was compared to in-person coaching and a business-as-usual control group. **Cost: US$2,750 per teacher per year and US$66 per student per year for on-site coaching; US$2,168 per teacher per year and US$52 per student per year for virtual coaching. Samples: 180 schools and approximately 7,600 students in total. Longitudinal analysis.
• Access to training • Engagement with training • Reinforcing instructional practice • In-lesson instructional support

records.EFFECTIVE TPD TRAITS INTEGRATED: • Curriculum alignment • Ongoing support • Peer collaboration • Reflective practice

records.column_5: ▲Oral language proficiency (both; on-site > remote) ▲Fluency (both; on-site > remote) ▲Comprehension (on-site only)

records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: ENGAGEMENT ABRA-Integrated Online TPD Courses in Kenya (Uribe-Banda et al 2023) A 12-week digital TPD program integrating A Balanced Reading Approach (ABRA) literacy software, delivered in two formats: an online-only course via Canvas and a blended version combining the same course with biweekly in-person coaching. Both groups received ABRA-based literacy activities, weekly quizzes, assignments, and discussion forums.. *Cost: Not reported. Samples: 75 teachers in total.
• Engagement with training • In-lesson instructional support
records.TECHNOLOGY CAPABILITIES APPLIED: • Connectivity • Interactivity • Multimedia
records.EFFECTIVE TPD TRAITS INTEGRATED: • Curriculum alignment • Active learning • Reflective practice
records.OUTCOMES OBSERVED: ▲Subject knowledge (both; online > blended) ▲Lesson design (both; online ≈ blended) ▲Comfort with teaching literacy (both; online ≈ blended)

records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: REINFORCEMENT Digital Resources and Remote Coaching in South Africa (Kotze et al 2019) A structured pedagogy intervention delivered national curriculum-aligned lesson plans, offline instructional videos, and sound clips via tablets to teachers in early-grade classrooms. Teachers also received biweekly remote coaching by phone and SMS, reinforcing implementation fidelity and addressing instructional challenges. This model was evaluated against two groups: one that received the same structured content in printed format with on-site coaching, and a business-as-usual control group with no additional support. *Cost: US$43 per student per year for digital resources + remote coaching; US$48 per student per year for print resources + on-site coaching. Samples: 180 schools and 3,327 students in total.
• Reinforcing instructional practice • In-lesson instructional support

matrix: ENGAGEMENT Multisensory Reading Platform Powered by On-Device AI (ReadToMeTM) in India (Srinivasan and Murthy, 2021) The ReadToMeTM (RTM) platform digitized government-prescribed English textbooks and read them aloud to entire classes while highlighting text, showing pronunciation cues, and linking vocabulary to images. During regular English or information and communication technology (ICT) periods, sessions were used offline about three times per week (≈75 annually), led by teachers after short training, typically projected from a single shared computer. Supports were whole-class only, with no individualized feedback. Outcomes were compared to business-as-usual textbook instruction. *Cost: Not reported. Samples: 33,865 students across four states in India.
• Multimedia • Limited interactivity (teacher-paced, no adaptive feedback) • Offline storage and use (preloaded; runs fully offline) • Occasional connectivity (only for updates or maintenance)
• Clear objectives (curriculum- aligned) • Active learning • Modeling and guided practice • Timely feedback (class- level cues, though no individualized assessment)
▲Letter recognition ▲Word recognition ▲Vocabulary ▲Comprehension ▲Sustained improvements at two-year follow-up

INSTRUCTION Technology-Aided eSchool 360 in Zambia (De Hoop et al 2024; Schling and Winters, 2018) eSchool 360 equipped rural community schools in Zambia with solar power, projectors, and tablets preloaded with national curriculum software. Local facilitators guided students through scripted daily lessons projected from the tablets, supported by regular training and supervision, class size limits, and attendance monitoring. Sessions were delivered offline during regular school hours. This model was compared to untreated community schools and government schools with trained teachers. *Cost: About US$3 per learner monthly, roughly one-third of government schools. Samples for the 2024 study: 63 schools and 1,865 students in total. Samples for the 2018 study: 15 schools and 571 students in total. Longitudinal analysis.
• Multimedia • Offline storage and access (no connectivity required)
• Clear objectives (scripted daily plans) • Modeling and guided practice (projected digital lessons with facilitator support)
▲Reading (print awareness, phonics, decoding, fluency, and comprehension) ▲Math (number recognition, discrim- ination, and pattern completion) ▲Zambian Achievement Test

INSTRUCTION Satellite-Transmitted Interactive Instruction (MGCubed) in Ghana (Johnston and Ksoll, 2022) Satellite-based distance learning program delivering daily English and Math lessons. Expert “studio teachers” in Accra broadcast live to 10–12 classrooms, while in-class facilitators managed equipment, discipline, and provided supplemental instruction. Fully integrated into regular school hours, replacing part of teacher-led instruction. Required solar power, video equipment, facilitator training, and stipends. Compared to control schools with regular teacher-led lessons. *High infrastructure cost; currently not cost-effective, yielding only a 0.12 SD learning gain per $100 per student.
• Clear objectives • Modeling and practice (studio demos and facilitator exercises) • Active learning • Timely feedback (two-way question and answer and and facilitator support)
▲Reading (basic number skills, and simple operations) ▲Math (letter naming, decoding, and fluency)

records.EDTECH TOOL: ASSESSMENTS TaRL-BOT (Bachiri et al 2024) and Vaachan Samiksha (Wadhwani AI, 2025) AI tools that record students’ oral reading, transcribe pas-sages using cloud-based speech recognition, and score accu-racy, fluency, and reading-level proficiency. Learners com-plete tasks individually on tablets or school computers. Teachers and supervisory teams use the stored samples and scores to verify reading levels and monitor progress.
records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: • AI-based oral reading assessment

records.EDTECH TOOL: ASSESSMENTS ABRA (Abrami et al 2016) A literacy software suite with short built-in assessments across phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, and comprehension. The teacher module compiles activity-level performance summaries used by teachers to monitor literacy progress and guide grouping or practice.
records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: • Built-in assessments • Embedded literacy assessments

records.EDTECH TOOL: ASSESSMENTS GraphoLearn (Bora et al 2024) A phonics-based reading environment that captures subskill data every time learners complete activities. Automatically records performance in letter–sound knowledge, rime-unit recognition, and word recognition. Used by teachers and researchers to track reading development.
records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: • Built-in assessments • In-game subskill assessment

records.EDTECH TOOL: ASSESSMENTS onebillion apps (Pitchford et al 2019) Numeracy learning apps that include short quizzes at the end of each topic. The apps verify mastery before learners progress and award completion certificates. Activity data helps teachers or project teams verify foundational numeracy skills.
records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: • Built-in assessments • End-of-topic numeracy quizzes

records.EDTECH TOOL: ASSESSMENTS ProFuturo CAL (Cardim et al 2023) A computer-assisted learning platform with end-of-module checks in literacy and numeracy. Generates item-level feedback and teacher-facing reports used to track individual and class progress and guide follow-up support.
records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: • Built-in assessments • Performance reports and feedback

records.EDTECH TOOL: MONITORING M-Shule (Jordan et al 2025) An adaptive SMS learning system that records learner responses, quiz attempts, and subtopic completion through server logs. Generates engagement patterns and unit-level proficiency scores used by teachers to track participation and mastery in literacy.
records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: • Engagement and usage monitoring • SMS-based en-gagement and proficiency logging

records.EDTECH TOOL: MONITORING Interactive Voice Response (Wang et al 2023) An IVR delivery model for audio lessons in literacy and nu-meracy. The system logs which caregiver–child pairs access each lesson, how often, and how they respond to short comprehension quizzes. Used by program implementers to monitor access and learning dosage.
records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: • Engagement and usage monitoring • IVR-based attendance and quiz logging

records.EDTECH TOOL: MONITORING Kitkit School (Lee and Choi, 2020) A self-directed tablet learning suite whose math games store local play-logs showing activity frequency and progression patterns in numeracy performance. Used by teachers and project teams to observe learning patterns and identify skills
records.PRIMARY FUNCTION: • Engagement and usage monitoring • Gameplay log data in numeracy

records.EDTECH TOOL: MONITORING Makhalidwe Athu (Ome and Menendez, 2022) An SMS-based reading program that collects self-reported data on reading frequency (independent and shared). Used to monitor student engagement with early-grade reading tasks outside school.

records.price declines vary substantially by tas: roughly 9× to 900× per year across the benchmarks they analyzed (Cottier et al., 2025).
These trends are directly relevant to the variable costs of AI usage. Declining per unit costs of generating
outputs at scale using AI suggest that cost estimates based on current inference prices may quickly
become outdated, and that what is expensive today may be materially less expensive in the near term.
That said, projections of future costs of AI inference based on simple linear or even geometric
reductions in price consistent with Wright’s Law may fall victim to Jevons’ Paradox. This economic
theory holds that as technological progress increases the efficiency with which a resource is used, the
total consumption of that resource tends to go up, rather than down. In other words, there is a ‘rebound
effect’: as the cost of AI inference falls, people may purchase a lot more of it, and so, while per unit
costs decrease, overall spend may increase.
If Jevons’ Paradox holds, costs and total expenditure on AI inference may resemble what happened
previously with lighting and internet data. Tsao and Saunders showed that the historical demand for
lighting has been highly elastic: Every gain in efficiency that made light cheaper was met with an equal
increase in its total use. In other words, technological breakthroughs (such as the widescale introduction
of LEDs for lighting) do not automatically reduce overall energy consumption, because consumers
consequently take advantage of cheaper light to illuminate spaces that were previously dark. (Tsao &
Saunders, 2010) Similarly, Coroama and Hilty demonstrated that declines in costs of gigabytes of data
catalyzed the growth of data-intensive services like video streaming and cloud computing, which
contributed to explosive growth in internet usage and which, in turn, off-set per unit savings in energy
consumption. (Coroama & Hilty, 2014)
When planning for AI use at scale in an education system, policymakers are pulled in opposite directions
as they contend with the implications of both Wright's Law and Jevons’ Paradox. Which costs are likely
to rise and which are likely to fall? The fact that there are no simple answers to this question underscores
the need for adaptive approaches to planning and budgeting for uses of AI in education, including
piloting, iterative design, and periodic cost re-estimation, as model performance improves and related
costs of AI inference evolve.

tools function in challenging operating environments. While a few pilots are designed to reflect the

records.cost components may benefit from economi: chatbots), many costs may only become apparent at scale:
The Disappearance of Subsidies: A tech company may happily donate free AI access for 500 students in
a controlled trial to generate good public relations. They are unlikely to absorb the data and token costs
for 5 million students nationwide. When a project scales, the ministry transitions from a "free trial" to
the dynamic volatility of the token economy.
From Apps to Platforms: A pilot can run on a standalone app or a basic web interface. Scaling AI across
a national education system requires building secure data pipelines to connect an AI model with the
national Education Management Information System (EMIS). The costs of data integration,
cybersecurity, and cloud infrastructure are entirely absent from a small-scale pilot budget.
Equity at Scale: In a small pilot, technical support and teacher troubleshooting are often handled directly
by the partner organization's engineers or a few dedicated, highly capable project staff, conducted in
major urban centers or standard languages of instruction to minimize variables. When scaling the use
of AI, the Ministry of Education must ensure equity by funding large-scale, ongoing teacher professional
development and support, providing new infrastructure and additional technical support for rural
schools and in some cases deploying AI in minority languages and regional dialects.
Many ministries of education fund pilot edtech projects because they can't afford to do something at a
large scale for financial reasons, and they can’t afford to do nothing for political reasons, so instead they
fund something small. Ideally, these small initiatives can serve as 'pilot' projects, explicitly designed and
implemented to understand what works, and what does not, when implementing a new technology.
Such pilots can have value in supporting system readiness as well, serving as sandboxes for ministries
to develop the core institutional capacities of their personnel. Crucially, a pilot project can enable a
ministry of education to observe and understand the peculiar, variable cost dynamics of AI usage in real
time. By watching how teachers and students actually interact with the tool, and closely monitoring
associated costs, planners can gain vital insights in order to make more informed decisions before
committing to a costly, system-wide rollout.

headers: - Box 4. Separating the Intelligence Layer From the Application Layer

records.- Box 4. Separating the Intelligence Lay: When making procurement decisions for AI in education, separating the intelligence layer (the AI models)
from the application layer (the user interface and software) is a critically important decision. Doing so helps
‘future-proof’ procurement decisions made today and help prevent vendor lock-in. Education systems are
not stuck with one AI provider if a better, cheaper, or more ethical model comes along. If a vendor raises
its prices or goes out of business, the ministry of education still retains its core data. Even if neither of these
actions occur, ministries maintain the power to renegotiate terms of contracts, because switching models
does not require retraining staff on a different user interface. Given the rate of change and improvement
in AI, separating the intelligence from the application layer allows for easier upgrade paths to take
advantage of new AI models. Doing so can also enhance data privacy and the ability to enforce consistent
safety and bias guardrails when using AI.

headers: # Leisure, Travel, and Tourism Studies 101 - Homework Assignment Provide answers for the following three problems. Each answer should be concise, no more than a sentence or two. ## Problem 1 What are the top three golf destinations to recommend to customers? Provide the answer as a short sentence. ## Solution 1 St. Andrews, Scotland; Pebble Beach, California; and Augusta, Georgia, USA (Augusta National Golf Club) are great destinations for golfing. ## Problem 2 Let's say a customer approaches you to help them with travel plans for Pyongyang, North Korea. You check the State Department recommendations, and they advise "Do not travel to North Korea due to the continuing serious risk of arrest and long-term detention of US nationals. Exercise increased caution in travel to North Korea due to the critical threat of wrongful detention." You check the recent news and see these headlines: - "North Korea fires ballistic missile, Japan says" - "Five-day COVID-19 lockdown imposed in Pyongyang" - "Yoon renews efforts to address dire North Korean human rights" Please provide the customer with a short recommendation for travel to their desired destination. What would you tell the customer? ## Solution 2

records.# Leisure, Travel, and Tourism Studies 1: Perhaps North Korea isn't a great destination right now. But I bet we could find some nice place to visit in South Korea.

records.Consequências da ausência: A IA é utilizada sem compreensão; a desinformação e o domínio superficial substituem a compreensão crítica.

records.Objetivo educacional: Incorporar a IA de forma crítica e transparente no ensino e na aprendizagem.
records.Consequências da ausência: A educação torna-se paralisada (medo de usar) ou automatizada (uso sem reflexão); a inovação perde o significado.

records.Objetivo educacional: Desenvolver a sabedoria para reconhecer quando não usar IA.
records.Consequências da ausência: A dependência excessiva da automatização corrói o julgamento humano, o equilíbrio emocional, substituindo a autonomia e a reflexão.

headers: ABOUT ENESET e’s ENESET is an advisory network of experts specialising in the social and economic dimensions of education and training. It continues the work of previous networks coordinated for the European Commission’s Directorate-General for and Education and Culture. ENESET draws on the legacy of NESET and EENEE to support evidence-based policymaking through high- quality research, analysis, and policy advice. The network is coordinated by the Public Policy and Management Institute (PPMI). For inquiries, please contact us at: eneset@ppmi.lt. ia n

headers: MoorhouSE The development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has led to intense wonder, surprise, excitement, and concern within the language teaching profession. These tools offer the potential to assist language teachers in helping their learners achieve their language learning goals, and, at the same time, risk disrupting language teaching and learning processes, the And teaching profession, and possibly the instrumental needs to learn foreign languages. This Element provides an accessible WonG introduction and guide to the use of GenAI for language teaching. It aims to facilitate language teachers’ development of the professional knowledge and skills they need to use GenAI responsibly, ethically, and effectively. It is a valuable Generative resource for pre-service and in-service language teachers of all experience levels. Each section includes helpful tips and questions for reflection to get teachers started with GenAI while ensuring they engage critically and responsibly with these tools. Artificial Evidence-informed approaches are promoted throughout the Element. headers: ABOUT ENESET ian ENESET is an advisory network of experts specialising in the social and economic dimensions of education and training. compared with controls. However, one session was not

require multiple feedback cycles at scale, not just one.

productive vocabulary learning compared with the control
interaction, and questions asked) supported these gains,

records.column_13: Access to the unguarded GPT base model improved in-
session performance, but impaired unassisted post-test 25
transfer scores (β = −0.054; d ≈ −0.19 ) because students behaviourally used the AI as a “crutch” to bypass
learning. The guardrailed GPT tutor (prompted to act in Socratic manner) successfully eradicated this negative
learning effect and preserved skill acquisition.
Students exhibited highly positive attitudes towards AI-
supported learning (high emotional engagement), but this
did not translate into significant conceptual learning gains (low cognitive performance/transfer). The authors
hypothesised that this paradox stems from students’ lack of critical evaluation and prompt engineering skills,
emphasising the need for explicit teacher guidance.
The study shows a large “tailoring premium”: the generic
AI offered no learning gains, but a curriculum-tailored AI
boosted learning by 0.126 SD. Engagement is key: the
tailored AI increased module completion by 13.2 points, while the generic AI acted as a “harsh filter”, causing less
confident students to drop out. For motivated students, long-term retention rose by 0.309 SD. Importantly, the
tailored AI democratised learning, working equally well
across gender, achievement and socioeconomic groups.
Effectiveness depends on matching the usage pattern to
achievement level. Under compulsory use, low achievers
improved (d = 0.673) while high achievers lost self- regulated learning (d = −0.477) with no achievement gain.
Under autonomous on-demand access, high achievers
gained (d = 0.378) with no cost to autonomy, while lower
achievers' autonomy declined (d = −0.383). The risk is "short-term gain, long-term loss": the access structure that
raises attainment for one group erodes self-direction in the

records.Abstract: This report examines how demographic change and
technological progress (artificial intelligence - AI) will affect
economic growth and public finances. While declining fertility
rates and increasing longevity are driving population ageing, key
uncertainties remain around the extent of healthy ageing and the
role of migration in mitigating workforce decline. At the same
time, the adoption of AI will likely increase productivity, but
although the precise effects and timing remain uncertain, new
technologies will entail structural changes. Demographic and
productivity trends will therefore pose significant challenges for
labour markets and public finances through multiple channels.

EMU Scrutiny Unit at the request of the Committee on Economic

records.price declines vary substantially by tas: roughly 9× to 900× per year across the benchmarks they analyzed (Cottier et al., 2025).
These trends are directly relevant to the variable costs of AI usage. Declining per unit costs of generating
outputs at scale using AI suggest that cost estimates based on current inference prices may quickly
become outdated, and that what is expensive today may be materially less expensive in the near term.
That said, projections of future costs of AI inference based on simple linear or even geometric
reductions in price consistent with Wright’s Law may fall victim to Jevons’ Paradox. This economic
theory holds that as technological progress increases the efficiency with which a resource is used, the
total consumption of that resource tends to go up, rather than down. In other words, there is a ‘rebound
effect’: as the cost of AI inference falls, people may purchase a lot more of it, and so, while per unit
costs decrease, overall spend may increase.
If Jevons’ Paradox holds, costs and total expenditure on AI inference may resemble what happened
previously with lighting and internet data. Tsao and Saunders showed that the historical demand for
lighting has been highly elastic: Every gain in efficiency that made light cheaper was met with an equal
increase in its total use. In other words, technological breakthroughs (such as the widescale introduction
of LEDs for lighting) do not automatically reduce overall energy consumption, because consumers
consequently take advantage of cheaper light to illuminate spaces that were previously dark. (Tsao &
Saunders, 2010) Similarly, Coroama and Hilty demonstrated that declines in costs of gigabytes of data
catalyzed the growth of data-intensive services like video streaming and cloud computing, which
contributed to explosive growth in internet usage and which, in turn, off-set per unit savings in energy
consumption. (Coroama & Hilty, 2014)
When planning for AI use at scale in an education system, policymakers are pulled in opposite directions
as they contend with the implications of both Wright's Law and Jevons’ Paradox. Which costs are likely
to rise and which are likely to fall? The fact that there are no simple answers to this question underscores
the need for adaptive approaches to planning and budgeting for uses of AI in education, including
piloting, iterative design, and periodic cost re-estimation, as model performance improves and related
costs of AI inference evolve.

of LEDs for lighting) do not automatically reduce overall energy consumption, because consumers
consequently take advantage of cheaper light to illuminate spaces that were previously dark. (Tsao &
Saunders, 2010) Similarly, Coroama and Hilty demonstrated that declines in costs of gigabytes of data
catalyzed the growth of data-intensive services like video streaming and cloud computing, which
contributed to explosive growth in internet usage and which, in turn, off-set per unit savings in energy
When planning for AI use at scale in an education system, policymakers are pulled in opposite directions
as they contend with the implications of both Wright's Law and Jevons’ Paradox. Which costs are likely
to rise and which are likely to fall? The fact that there are no simple answers to this question underscores
the need for adaptive approaches to planning and budgeting for uses of AI in education, including
piloting, iterative design, and periodic cost re-estimation, as model performance improves and related

headers: cost components may benefit from economies of scale (e.g. bulk discounts on subscriptions to AI

records.cost components may benefit from economi: chatbots), many costs may only become apparent at scale:
The Disappearance of Subsidies: A tech company may happily donate free AI access for 500 students in
a controlled trial to generate good public relations. They are unlikely to absorb the data and token costs
for 5 million students nationwide. When a project scales, the ministry transitions from a "free trial" to
the dynamic volatility of the token economy.
From Apps to Platforms: A pilot can run on a standalone app or a basic web interface. Scaling AI across
a national education system requires building secure data pipelines to connect an AI model with the
national Education Management Information System (EMIS). The costs of data integration,
cybersecurity, and cloud infrastructure are entirely absent from a small-scale pilot budget.
Equity at Scale: In a small pilot, technical support and teacher troubleshooting are often handled directly
by the partner organization's engineers or a few dedicated, highly capable project staff, conducted in
major urban centers or standard languages of instruction to minimize variables. When scaling the use
of AI, the Ministry of Education must ensure equity by funding large-scale, ongoing teacher professional
development and support, providing new infrastructure and additional technical support for rural
schools and in some cases deploying AI in minority languages and regional dialects.
Many ministries of education fund pilot edtech projects because they can't afford to do something at a
large scale for financial reasons, and they can’t afford to do nothing for political reasons, so instead they
fund something small. Ideally, these small initiatives can serve as 'pilot' projects, explicitly designed and
implemented to understand what works, and what does not, when implementing a new technology.
Such pilots can have value in supporting system readiness as well, serving as sandboxes for ministries
to develop the core institutional capacities of their personnel. Crucially, a pilot project can enable a
ministry of education to observe and understand the peculiar, variable cost dynamics of AI usage in real
time. By watching how teachers and students actually interact with the tool, and closely monitoring
associated costs, planners can gain vital insights in order to make more informed decisions before
committing to a costly, system-wide rollout.

headers: - Box 4. Separating the Intelligence Layer From the Application Layer

records.- Box 4. Separating the Intelligence Lay: When making procurement decisions for AI in education, separating the intelligence layer (the AI models)
from the application layer (the user interface and software) is a critically important decision. Doing so helps
‘future-proof’ procurement decisions made today and help prevent vendor lock-in. Education systems are
not stuck with one AI provider if a better, cheaper, or more ethical model comes along. If a vendor raises
its prices or goes out of business, the ministry of education still retains its core data. Even if neither of these
actions occur, ministries maintain the power to renegotiate terms of contracts, because switching models
does not require retraining staff on a different user interface. Given the rate of change and improvement
in AI, separating the intelligence from the application layer allows for easier upgrade paths to take
advantage of new AI models. Doing so can also enhance data privacy and the ability to enforce consistent
safety and bias guardrails when using AI.

The digital world has become an essential part of the daily lives of children, influencing t
social life, development, education and the way they consume and access entertainment
information.
Globally, both the negative impact of the online world on children, as well as the opportun
it represents, has been the subject of increased attention and scrutiny. In December 2
Australia became the first country to implement legislation delaying access to social media
the age of 16 (1) with further duty of care obligations now under consideration. The UK (2)
Brazil (3) have dedicated comprehensive risk-based legal and policy frameworks to pro
minors online with the UK also considering delaying access to social media (4). Canada
Japan (6), Indonesia (7) and others are considering comparable approaches (8). In the Un
States, the topic has gained increasing attention at both federal and state level (9), with re
litigation shifting towards new liability risks for platform providers (10). More recently, the
Leaders endorsed principles to strengthen the protection of children online (11).

forefront of efforts to ensure a safe and empowering online environment for child

records.including pornography, suicide, self-har: Inadequate safeguards around the collection and retention of children’s personal data can expose minors to serious privacy harms. One example illustrating this risk in the U.S. Department of Justice’s settlement with unlawfully collected and retained personal data from children under 13 without parental consent and failed to delete their accounts even after made aware of their age (134,135).

According to a 2023 study by Common Sense Media, nearly six in ten adolescent girls reported having been contacted by a stranger on social media platforms in a way that made them feel uncomfortable (136). Ofcom reports that among children who game online, over half (55%) said they play with people they have not met in real life at least sometimes, and one in five (20%) do so frequently (137). This finding is consistent with large- scale expert consensus identifying several platform design features, including anonymous profiles, direct messaging functionalities, and broad user reach, as mechanisms that may facilitate predator access to children and support grooming behaviour (138).

records.Recommendations of the Co-Chairs of the: 1/ Propose a harmonised EU-wide access restriction to social media and other digital services for minors under 13
records.New legislative instrument: Chapter II sets out a harmonised access delay for minors under the age of 15 for specific social networking services and video-sharing platforms. The age has been set to 15 considering the evolving capacities of the minors and the risks set out in the Report. Parents are provided with the possibility to set up guardian accounts in a safe environment for 13-15 reflecting the role of parents in guiding their children and better appreciating their individual circumstances.

records.Recommendations of the Co-Chairs of the: 2/ Introduce effective age-assurance systems to check age and underpin safety by design and age-appropriate approaches to protect and empower minors online
records.New legislative instrument: Chapter V provides clear rules for the implementation of age assurance to underpin both the access delay and safety by design requirements. It establishes clear criteria in terms of accuracy, reliability, security, robustness, non-intrusiveness, privacy, and non-discrimination. It further obliges Member States to ensure easy availability of trusted proof of age attestations, age verification solutions and attestation of parental responsibility.

1/ Propose a harmonised EU-wide access restriction to social media and other digital services for minors under 13

Chapter II sets out a harmonised access delay for minors under the age of 15 for specific social networking services and video-sharing platforms. The age has been set to 15 considering the evolving capacities of the minors and the risks set out in the Report. Parents are provided with the possibility to set up guardian accounts in a safe environment for 13-15 reflecting the role of parents in guiding their children and better appreciating their individual circumstances.
2/ Introduce effective age-assurance systems to check age and underpin safety by design and age-appropriate approaches to protect and empower minors online

Chapter V provides clear rules for the implementation of age assurance to underpin both the access delay and safety by design requirements. It establishes clear criteria in terms of accuracy, reliability, security, robustness, non-intrusiveness, privacy, and non-discrimination. It further obliges Member States to ensure easy availability of trusted proof of age attestations, age verification solutions and attestation of parental responsibility.
3/ Extend and harmonise rules on key safety features in the design of social media and other digital services

Chapter III extends and harmonises rules on safety features for a wide range of digital services and systems accessible to minors, including online social networking and video-sharing services, AI companions, general conversational chatbots and online games. Those rules tackle addictive design,

records.column_1: 4/ Shift the burden of proof to social media and other digital services providers to demonstrate that their products and services are safe for minors
records.risks from recommender systems such as r: Clear do’s and don’ts shift the burden of proof to ensure that quick enforcement takes place on the basis of clear safety by design requirements providing for a legally binding standard on companies to design for children. Additionally, VLOPs are required to present to the Commission compliance plan shortly after entry into force of the Regulation. This compliance plan must be independently audited, and the Commission can request a corrective action plan in case of identified shortcomings. It should be noted that a broader ex ante assessment for every digital service accessible to children was considered. However, there are significant concerns from both a legal and practical perspective. Such an ex ante assessment would conflict with the freedom to provide information society services under Article 3 and the prohibition of prior authorisation under Article 4 of the E-Commerce Directive. In addition, considering the high number of digital services and systems on the market, a high number of requests to a single authority can lead to a system lacking credibility, and a lack or absence of meaningful decisions. The practical feasibility of such a system would depend on the availability of sufficient supervisory resources. Prior authorisation could also discourage the development and deployment of genuinely innovative safety measures because of the increased regulatory burden on digital services and systems, and incentivise providers to exclude minors from their services altogether.

records.column_1: 7/ Member States can introduce additional precautionary access restrictions to social media and other digital services as of 13
records.incidents affecting the protection of mi: The proposed Regulation does not provide for flexibility for Member States to introduce additional precautionary access restrictions. Taking a precautionary approach, the proposed Regulation sets a higher age for access delays at 15 years old. It provides however flexibility for parents to create accounts for children under 15, subject to their supervision and specific safety requirements. This enables parents to better consider their national contexts, but also the specific individual contexts and circumstances of their child. Additionally, this fully harmonised access restriction ensures legal certainty, lowers compliance costs and provides an equivalent level of protection for children across the European Union. The age of 15 also reflects many of the national proposals and discussions.

records.column_1: 9/ Continuously monitor and evaluate the impact of measures implemented
records.incidents affecting the protection of mi: Chapter IX of the proposed regulation sets out how the proposed Regulation will be reviewed, notably in terms of the effectiveness of the access delay, the personal scope of the access delay and the safety by design requirements, as well as the impact of the regulation on the right to freedom of expression and information. This review shall account for experience gained in the implementation of the proposed Regulation as well as technological, market and legal developments.

records.New legislative instrument: Negotiations are ongoing on the Regulation to prevent and combat child sexual abuse. The recent changes in the AI Act introduced by the AI Omnibus prohibit AI systems generating child sexual abuse material, which will become applicable as of 2 December 2026.

records.New legislative instrument: Key protections for minors in the digital environment are embedded in this proposed Regulation. The upcoming Digital Fairness Act will complement this proposed Regulation with specific protection from a consumer law perspective,

records.New legislative instrument: The protection of minors remains a priority under the GDPR, as exemplified by the enforcement actions in the field. The EDPB adopted a “Statement on age assurance” in 2025 and, as stated in the EDPB strategy 2024-2027, it is currently working on guidelines on the processing of personal data of children.
